Buildathon 2026 Participant Guide

This is your operating guide for the Bengaluru Tech Week Buildathon. Read it before arrival, keep it open during the build, and use the final checklist before you submit. The submission deadline is 3:00 PM IST.
Your day
Time
What happens
What you should do
8:00–9:00
Breakfast, check-in and setup
Arrive early. Confirm your team, laptop, power, GitHub access, development tools and optional Databricks Free Edition access.
9:00–12:00
Kickoff and build session
Choose one Entire track, fork only after the official start, configure the required Entire workflow, build a narrow end-to-end slice and create your early checkpoints.
12:00–1:00
The Noon Curveball and lunch
Stop, preserve your last stable version, close the current agent session, receive the new constraint, start fresh and reconstruct the project from checkpoint context before editing.
1:00–3:00
Build session and submission
Implement the constraint, test the changed behavior, verify the Entire Graph evidence, create the final checkpoint, finish BUILDATHON.md and submit before 3:00 PM.
3:00–5:00
Judging and winner announcement
Keep the project runnable. Mentors complete first-level review; eight finalists present; judges deliberate and awards are announced.


What makes this Buildathon different
You are not being asked to produce a generic app around a prompt. You must build a useful developer product on one of three Entire open-source surfaces, preserve decision context through checkpoints, use structural evidence from the Entire Graph where required, and respond to an additional non-negotiable constraint revealed at noon.
Teams may also make Databricks essential to the same product and opt in to the separate Best Use of Databricks awards. There remains one project and one submission; a team may win both an Entire main-challenge prize and a Databricks award.
Before you arrive
Bring and verify
A laptop, charger and any adapters you need. Bring a power bank only as a backup; do not rely on it for the full day.
A working GitHub account with permission to create forks and push to your fork.
Your preferred coding agent and local development tools already installed and signed in.
A local runtime that can run tests and a browser or API client that can demonstrate the product.
A Databricks Free Edition account if your team wants to compete for Best Use of Databricks. Create and open it before the event so account issues do not consume your build window.
A fallback demo asset: a recent screenshot or short screen recording for any step that depends on a live service.
Allowed before 9:00 AM
Research, user discovery, problem framing, sketches and planning are allowed before the official start. Implementation must begin after 9:00 AM on 6 September. Do not arrive with a prebuilt solution, completed feature branch or reusable implementation that gives your team an unfair head start.
Team readiness
Name one person as submission owner. This person checks every link and submits before 3:00 PM.
Name one person as the final demo owner. They should be able to explain the system even if another teammate wrote most of the code.
If using Databricks, choose one final demo workspace and one deployment owner. Use Git for shared code; never store secrets in the repository.
Agree how you will record decisions, failures and verified outcomes in checkpoints and BUILDATHON.md.
Account links
Create or open Databricks Free Edition
Buildathon details and updates
Bengaluru Tech Week Code of Conduct







Choose one Entire innovation track
Your team must select one track. The project should solve a real developer or agent-workflow problem and make Entire essential to the solution. Adding Entire only for tracking, without using its context, checkpoints or graph evidence to improve the product, will not qualify.
Track 1 — Build a Checkpoint-Native Developer Experience
Build a developer tool or workflow powered by context preserved in Entire Checkpoints. Git shows what changed; checkpoints should preserve why a change happened, what the agent attempted, which assumptions were made, what failed and what remains unresolved.
Review an implementation against its stated intent.
Identify unfinished requirements or unresolved risks.
Create a change-risk or release-readiness report.
Hand work to another developer or agent without losing the original reasoning.
Resume an agent-assisted workflow with confidence after a break.
Success looks like this: checkpoint context is an essential input, and a developer or agent completes a useful task more accurately or efficiently than they could from a Git diff alone.
Track 2 — Build with Graph Intelligence
Use the Entire Graph’s structural view of a codebase to support a useful decision or action. The graph can surface definitions, call relationships, types, routes and semantic changes. Your product must turn that evidence into a workflow that a developer or agent can inspect and verify.
Impact-aware code review or change-risk analysis.
Test selection based on affected relationships.
Migration planning or dependency-aware refactoring.
Codebase onboarding and guided exploration.
Combining Entire Graph findings with checkpoint intent.
Raw graph output is not enough. Your product should produce a useful decision, recommendation or workflow, show where the evidence came from, and let the user verify it against source code or tests.
Track 3 — Bring Entire to a New Agent or Workflow
Extend or create an Entire integration for a coding agent, editor, development environment, CI process or software-delivery workflow. The integration must capture meaningful development context and keep working in its intended operating mode.
Support for a new coding agent or editor workflow.
A CI or pull-request workflow that uses checkpoint context.
A multi-agent coordination workflow.
A protocol adapter between Entire and another developer tool.
External SDKs and fixtures are allowed, but the submitted implementation must live in the designated Entire fork. Calling an Entire command from another interface is not sufficient by itself.

Required Entire workflow
Complete these steps after the 9:00 AM kickoff. All implementation must happen in the clone created through the Entire mirror workflow.
1. Fork your selected repository
Fork the repository associated with your chosen track only after the Buildathon begins. Use existing issues for inspiration, or propose an original feature, integration or workflow.
2. Sign in and create the mirror
entire login
entire repo mirror create
entire repo clone /gh/YOUR-GITHUB-HANDLE/REPOSITORY
Select your fork and the India region when prompted. Clone through Entire, then work inside that clone.
3. Enable checkpoints
entire enable -y --agent YOUR-BUILD-AGENT
entire status
Commit meaningful milestones so code and context remain connected. Your checkpoint history must include at least:
Initial understanding and intended architecture.
The last stable state before the Noon Curveball.
Your response to the Noon Curveball.
Final implementation and verification.
Checkpoint quality matters more than quantity. Capture decisions, rejected options, failures, assumptions, open risks and the evidence that changed your approach.
4. Activate Entire Graph
entire plugin install graph
entire graph version
entire graph init-agents --repo .
Start a fresh agent session after activation so the agent receives the graph instructions. During development, show at least:
A graph search or definition lookup.
A relationship or impact analysis before a high-risk change.
A final semantic diff analysis of the submitted implementation.
Graph results are evidence, not an oracle. Verify findings against source code, tests and runtime behavior. Never present incomplete or uncertain graph output as a fact.

The Noon Curveball
At exactly 12:00 noon, every team receives an additional track-specific constraint that becomes mandatory. The first version is the proof of what you built. The second version is the proof that your process can absorb change without losing intent.
11:45 AM — preserve the stable state
Stop adding optional features and get the product back to a runnable state.
Commit the last stable version.
Create the required pre-noon Entire Checkpoint.
Record the current intent, architecture, completed work, unresolved work and important technical risks.
12:00 PM — receive the constraint
Stop implementation and close the current coding-agent session.
Receive the official Curveball from the organising team. Do not exchange cards or use another track’s instruction.
Start a fresh agent session and use checkpoint context to reconstruct the project before editing.
Run Entire Graph impact analysis before changing the affected area.
Implement the smallest complete response, test it and record the result in a new checkpoint.
What judges will look for
A strong response preserves the product’s core idea, changes a real architectural or reliability decision, uses checkpoint context accurately, uses graph evidence where relevant, remains testable and explains why the revised behavior can be trusted.
The Curveball’s specific instructions are intentionally not published in advance. Mentors and organisers must not disclose them before noon.

Competing for Best Use of Databricks
Databricks is an additional award category within the same project.
Free Edition setup
Each teammate may explore in an individual Databricks Free Edition workspace.
Choose one final workspace for the shared dataset, deployed app or endpoint and final demonstration.
Keep notebooks, app code, configuration and documentation in the shared Git repository. Never commit access tokens or credentials.
Name one deployment owner and test that the owner can sign in and open every required resource before judging.
Good scope for a one-day build
An AI app or agent using Databricks Apps, hosted foundation models, model serving or AI Search where available.
An analytics experience using notebooks, SQL, dashboards or Genie to answer a concrete question.
A data pipeline that ingests, cleans and transforms representative data into a useful result.
A data-backed application using Lakehouse data and Databricks Apps for the user experience.
An ML experiment that uses a reproducible dataset, experiment tracking and an evaluation result.
Free Edition constraints to design around
Area
Planning constraint
Service model
No-cost, serverless, quota-limited environment for non-commercial learning and prototyping; no production SLA.
SQL and jobs
One serverless 2X-Small SQL warehouse; up to five concurrent job tasks per account.
Pipelines
One active pipeline per supported pipeline type.
Models and AI Search
Endpoint, throughput and model availability limits apply; no GPU or provisioned throughput; AI Search is limited.
Apps and database
Up to three Apps, with idle auto-stop behavior; one Lakebase project where available.
Workspace
One workspace and one metastore per account; several account-level and enterprise controls are unavailable.
Quota
When quota is exhausted, affected compute may be unavailable for the rest of the day or month. Build and test your narrow path early.


Work locally when practical, deploy one narrow slice early and preserve a screenshot or recording of any fragile live step. If live infrastructure fails during judging, explain the expected behavior, show the prepared evidence and continue with the product story.
Databricks Free Edition overview
Current Databricks Free Edition limitations
Responsible use of AI and data
Do not upload confidential company information, customer data, passwords, private keys or personal data that you do not have permission to use.
Do not put secrets in prompts, source repositories, screenshots, checkpoint context or BUILDATHON.md.
Verify generated code, SQL, citations and outputs. Test the cases that matter to your user and disclose what remains unverified.
Explain your data sources, permitted use, sampling or transformation, and important limitations.
Clearly label synthetic, cached, mocked or prototype data and responses.
You remain accountable for the implementation, even when a coding agent created it. Every teammate presenting should understand the relevant code and product decisions.

Final 20-minute checklist
The final commit is pushed and the SHA matches the submission.
The project launches from a clean checkout or the documented setup path.
Required checkpoints open and clearly explain the four milestones.
Entire Graph evidence and the final semantic-diff analysis are recorded.
BUILDATHON.md is complete, readable and free of secrets.
Tests covering the critical and Curveball behavior pass.
Databricks resource links and data notes are included if you opted in.
The demo owner can sign in, open every resource and run the critical path.
A fallback screenshot or recording is locally available.
The submission is sent before 3:00 PM IST.

Code of Conduct and safety
All participants must follow the Bengaluru Tech Week Code of Conduct. Treat teammates, organisers, mentors, judges, venue staff and other participants with respect. Report harassment, unsafe behavior, accessibility barriers or urgent welfare issues to the event desk. For non-urgent questions, write to hello@bengalurutechweek.com.
Read the Bengaluru Tech Week Code of Conduct



Submission package
Submit one project before 3:00 PM IST. Late or incomplete submissions may not reach judging. Open every link in a private or signed-out browser where appropriate, and make sure judges have the access they need without receiving a private credential.
Required submission fields
Selected Entire track.
GitHub fork URL and final commit SHA.
Entire mirror or project URL.
Links to the required Entire Checkpoints.
Clear setup, run and test instructions.
Working product demonstration or a reliable fallback recording.
A complete BUILDATHON.md file in the repository root.
If opting into Best Use of Databricks: the Databricks capabilities used, why they are essential, workspace/app/endpoint/demo URL, relevant repository paths, reproduction steps, data provenance and how the Curveball affected the Databricks workflow.

BULDATHON.md outline
# Project name
## One-sentence summary
## Problem, intended user and why it matters
## Selected Entire track and why Entire is essential
## Architecture and main workflow
## Entire Graph findings and verification
## Noon Curveball: what changed and how we adapted
## Checkpoint links and what each checkpoint proves
## Setup, run and test instructions
## Databricks use, data sources and limitations (if applicable)
## Known limitations and next steps

Final demo readiness
State the user and problem in one sentence.
Show the working product and the critical path, rather than a slide-only walkthrough.
Explain why Entire is essential to the solution.
Show one useful checkpoint and one graph finding that changed or verified a decision.
Explain the Noon Curveball, the behavior that changed and the test that proves it.
If opting into Databricks, show the essential Databricks function and the evidence that it is working.
Close with known limitations and the next step toward production readiness.

Read both. Here's my honest read, then a sharper plan.

## Which doc is better

They're not competing — they're two different artifacts, and both are incomplete on their own.

| | `GATE_CLAUDE_CODE_PROMPT.md` | `GATE_CONTEXT.md` |
|---|---|---|
| What it is | Operational prompt pack (how to drive the agent) | Strategy/design doc (what to build and why) |
| Strong | Time-sliced discipline, evidence capture, "show me the signature or say you can't find it" | Verdict model (verified/unchecked/unusable), positioning, risk table, pitch lines |
| Weak | Verdict model is naive (3 states); front-loads too much scope for 2h45 | Hedges on Go vs Python and on in-fork vs CLI-wrapper — that ambiguity is dangerous |

**Merge, don't pick.** Take CONTEXT's thinking + PROMPT's operating discipline. But two things in CONTEXT need fixing before you paste anything:

1. **Kill the Python option.** Track rules: *"the submitted implementation must live in the designated Entire fork"* and *"calling an Entire command from another interface is not sufficient by itself."* A Python wrapper shelling out to `entire graph` is the exact failure mode named in the guide. Build it in Go, as `entire graph gate`, inside the fork. Non-negotiable.
2. **Drop the "adapted from Mirror" framing.** Borrowing design principles is fine; writing it in your submission doc invites a "did you bring prebuilt work?" question you don't want at 3pm. Keep the ideas, drop the lineage note.

## The problem with Gate as currently specced

Look at the Track 2 bullet list in the guide:

> Impact-aware code review or **change-risk analysis**. **Test selection based on affected relationships**. Migration planning. Onboarding. **Combining Entire Graph findings with checkpoint intent.**

Gate as written is bullets 1 and 2 — the two most obvious ones. Half the room builds blast-radius-plus-test-selection. With everyone holding Codex and Claude credits, code volume is not your moat. You will be one of six change-risk tools and the judges will remember whichever one had the sharpest *idea*.

Bullet 5 is the one almost nobody will do, because it requires understanding checkpoints *and* the graph. And it's the one that's worth points in **two** rubric rows (Graph 15 + Checkpoints 15).

## What I'd change: make intent divergence the headline

Reframe Gate from *"what does this change put at risk?"* to:

> **"Did the agent do what it said it was doing — and what did it put at risk along the way?"**

Concretely, one new signal that becomes the lead finding:

```
INTENT DIVERGENCE
  Stated intent: "fix pagination off-by-one in list endpoint"
  Intent-implied code regions (via graph search):  handlers/list.go, pager.go
  Entities changed outside that set:
    ✗ auth.VerifyToken      @ internal/auth/token.go:88   14 dependents, 0 tests
    ✗ config.Load           @ internal/config/load.go:31    6 dependents
  → 2 of 7 changed entities are unexplained by the stated intent.
```

Why this is the right bet:

- **It's deterministic.** `search` is a deterministic ranker. You take the checkpoint's intent text → search → ranked region set → set-difference against the entities the diff says actually changed. No LLM anywhere. Your "run it twice, identical bytes" pitch survives intact.
- **The checkpoint becomes load-bearing.** Right now in both your docs the checkpoint is just a way to name a commit range — remove it and Gate still works, which quietly fails the "Entire must be essential" test. With intent divergence, the checkpoint's *text* is an input to a signal. Remove it and the headline feature dies.
- **It's the failure mode people actually have with agents.** Everyone in that room has had an agent "fix the test" and quietly refactor three other files. That's the demo that gets a laugh of recognition.
- **It's cheap.** Search already exists inside the fork. You're calling it and doing set arithmetic.

Both your docs already have this — buried as stretch goal `--task` at the very bottom. Promote it to the front.

Two more cheap things that map word-for-word onto rubric language:

- **`--explain <finding-id>`** → prints the graph path (`A → calls → B → calls → C`) with file:line at each hop. The guide literally says *"let the user verify it against source code or tests."* Hand a judge a finding and invite them to falsify it.
- **`gate --json | shasum` twice** → identical. 15-second determinism proof.

Keep CONTEXT's **verified / unchecked / unusable** three-state model. It's the strongest idea in either doc and it's ~1 hour. "A changed symbol with no test isn't passing, it's unchecked" is a line judges will repeat.

## The thing neither doc exploits: you have two agents

You mentioned Codex credits *and* Claude. Both docs assume one sequential agent, which is why the 9:00–11:45 budget doesn't close. Run the numbers on the PROMPT doc's plan: subcommand+collect (50m) + reverse index & BFS (40m) + verdict/render (30m) + tests (25m) = 2h25 with a 20-minute buffer and **zero room** for companion gap or intent.

CONTEXT's one-direction architecture is what fixes this — but treat it as a **parallelization plan**, not an aesthetic choice:

**9:30 — write `types.go` first and commit it.** All structs: `ChangedEntity`, `Anchor`, `Finding`, `RiskReport`, `IntentReport`, `CompanionReport`, `Verdict`. That commit is the contract.

Then split:

| Agent A (Claude, needs repo knowledge) | Agent B (Codex, pure functions, zero repo knowledge) |
|---|---|
| `gate` subcommand registration + flags | `companions.go` — git log co-occurrence |
| `collect.go` — reuse the existing diff engine | `verdict.go` — pure, findings → verdict + exit code |
| `index.go` + `risk.go` — reverse edges, BFS depth ≤2 | `render.go` — text + `--json` |
| `intent.go` — call search internals | all unit tests against synthetic records |

Agent B never touches `internal/sem` and never needs to understand tree-sitter. Different files, no merge conflicts. Merge at 11:00, integrate 11:00–11:30, freeze 11:45. That's how four analysers fit where one doc budgets two.

## Revised schedule with hard cut lines

| Time | What | Cut line if late |
|---|---|---|
| 9:00–9:20 | Fork, mirror, clone, `entire enable`, plugin install, **`mise run build` immediately** (CGO first build is the #1 toolchain risk — find out at 9:05, not 10:30) | — |
| 9:20–9:35 | Recon: answer 4 questions with real file paths + signatures (where subcommands register / how to get entity diff / how to get symbol+relation records / how to call search internally) | — |
| 9:35–9:50 | `PLAN.md` + `types.go` committed → **Checkpoint 1** | — |
| 9:50–11:00 | Parallel build per table above | — |
| 11:00–11:30 | Integrate, end-to-end run, tests green | Drop companion gap |
| 11:30–11:45 | Freeze, `docs/how-gate-works.md`, **run Gate on itself and save output** → **Checkpoint 2** | Never cut this |
| 12:00–12:15 | Fresh session, reconstruct from checkpoint, restate constraint, graph impact analysis, **screenshot** | — |
| 12:15–14:15 | Curveball, smallest complete response + tests → **Checkpoint 3** | — |
| 14:15–14:40 | Run Gate on your own curveball commit, final `entire graph diff`, BUILDATHON.md → **Checkpoint 4** | — |
| 14:40 | Stop. Test checkpoint links **signed out**. | — |

Two risks both docs underrate: the CGO/tree-sitter first build, and reusing `internal/` APIs that may not be shaped for you. On the second — if the internal functions are awkward, dispatching through the existing internal CLI layer in-process is still *inside the fork* and still qualifies. Decide that by 9:35, don't fight it at 10:30.

## Where I'd put the demo

Not a slide. A terminal:

1. `git push` → **refused** by the pre-push hook, verdict `revert`, exit 2.
2. Point at the one finding: symbol, file:line, 14 dependents, zero tests.
3. `gate --explain 1` → the call path. Judge opens the file. It's true.
4. `gate --json | shasum` twice → same hash. "It never guesses."
5. Then run it on your own curveball commit, live.

---

Three decisions change what I write next, so let me get them from you:

Good — 3 builders + agents changes the math a lot. Let me argue the headline properly, since that's the one thing that decides whether you're memorable or the fourth change-risk tool of the day.

## The case for and against intent divergence

**How it actually works, mechanically:**

```
intent text → graph search → ranked regions (scored)
diff        → changed entities
join        → each changed entity gets a "how well does the stated intent explain this?" score
```

The output isn't a binary accusation. It's an ordering:

```
INTENT COVERAGE — "fix pagination off-by-one in list endpoint"
  rank  entity                      score   
  1     handlers.List               0.91    explained
  2     pager.Offset                0.88    explained
  3     pager.clamp                 0.71    explained
  ...
  6     config.Load                 0.09    UNEXPLAINED   6 dependents
  7     auth.VerifyToken            0.04    UNEXPLAINED  14 dependents, 0 tests
```

That framing matters — you're sorting evidence, not making a claim you can be wrong about. Much harder for a judge to break.

**The three real risks, and why each is survivable:**

| Risk | Reality | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|
| Can you even get intent text out of a checkpoint? | **Unknown until 9:20 recon.** This is the one thing that could kill it. | Fallback ladder: checkpoint intent → commit message subject+body → `--task "<text>"` flag. All three demo fine. `--task` alone is ~20 lines. Risk is contained. |
| Threshold is hand-tuned | Yes, genuinely. A diffuse intent ("refactor error handling") produces diffuse search results and false "unexplained" flags. | Never let divergence alone trigger `revert`. Divergence → `continue` at most. `revert` requires divergence **AND** dependents **AND** no tests. And if the intent text is too short/low-signal, that signal returns `unusable` — which is exactly what CONTEXT's exit code 5 is for. Disclose the threshold in the output itself. |
| It's extra scope | ~45–60 min if search internals are callable | With 3 builders, affordable. |

**The case against:** blast radius is more defensible, more obviously "graph intelligence," and won't look flaky live.

**My call:** you need blast radius regardless — it's the spine of the verdict, it's where the 15 graph points live, and it can't be cut. So the question isn't "risk *or* intent," it's whether intent ships as a headline or dies as a stretch goal. Given 3 builders and a contained failure mode, ship it. **Risk is the substance, intent is the framing.** The pitch becomes:

> Git shows what changed. Gate shows whether the agent did what it said, what that change puts at risk, what to test, and whether to trust it — and it never guesses.

The `--task` fallback means you can commit to this now and still be safe if checkpoint text isn't exposed. I wouldn't hedge with "add it by 11:00" — hedged features get cut, and the hedge costs you the framing you'd build the whole demo around.

## Three-builder split

The one rule that makes this work: **B1 ships stub `collect` returning hardcoded fixture records by 9:50.** Then B2 and B3 are unblocked from minute one and never wait on tree-sitter.

| | Owner | Files | Touches `internal/`? |
|---|---|---|---|
| **B1** | deepest repo knowledge, Claude in main clone | subcommand registration, flags, `collect.go` — entity diff, snapshot records, `runSearch(query)` | **Yes — only person who does** |
| **B2** | Codex, separate worktree | `index.go` (reverse-edge map), `risk.go` (BFS depth ≤2), `intent.go` | No — pure over B1's structs |
| **B3** | Codex, separate worktree | `companions.go` (git log), `verdict.go`, `render.go`, all unit tests | No repo knowledge at all |

B3's whole surface is pure functions over synthetic records — that person could work on a laptop that can't even build the repo. That's your insurance against CGO toolchain trouble.

**9:35–9:50 is the highest-leverage 15 minutes of the day:** write and commit `types.go` — `ChangedEntity`, `Anchor`, `Finding`, `RiskReport`, `IntentReport`, `CompanionReport`, `Verdict`, `SearchHit`. That commit is the contract three people code against. Get it wrong and you spend 11:00–11:30 in merge hell instead of integrating.

Two staffing notes from the rules: every presenter must be able to explain the code, so make the **demo owner the person who wrote the least** — they'll be forced to actually understand it, and it's the strongest signal to judges. And name the submission owner now; that person checks the checkpoint links in a signed-out browser at 14:40, not 14:58.

## What's still open

1. **Recon can start whenever you're clear to.** Reading the repo is research, which the guide allows pre-9:00 — but nothing lands in the repo until after kickoff. If you want, I'll run the four recon questions right now and come back with real file paths and function signatures: where `commit`/`diff`/`checkpoint` register, how to get entity-change records for base..head, how to get symbol+relation records, and whether search internals are callable in-process. That's the input to `types.go`.

# 1. The plan, in one page

**Gate** — one command, one verdict, on an agent's checkpoint.

**Five layers, one direction, no loops:**

| Layer | Job | Pure? |
|---|---|---|
| `collect` | checkpoint/refs → entity diff + snapshot records + search hits | No — only layer touching `internal/` |
| `index` | reverse-edge map, file→symbol map, keyed by compound-v1 IDs | Yes |
| `signals` | `risk()`, `intent()`, `coverage()`, `companions()` → findings with anchors | Yes |
| `verdict` | findings → verdict + exit code | Yes |
| `render` | text / `--json` | Yes |

**Four signals:**

1. **Intent** — does the stated intent explain each changed entity? (scored, ordered)
2. **Risk** — blast radius of removed/signature-changed entities, reverse edges, BFS depth ≤2
3. **Coverage** — verified / **unchecked** / no-resolver, + one runnable test command
4. **Companion gap** — files that habitually co-change but didn't this time

**Four verdicts:** `keep` 0 · `continue` 1 · `revert` 2 · `unusable` 5

# 3. So what's the actual standout factor?

Let me be blunt about where the points are.

**30 of 100 points (Checkpoints 15 + Graph 15) are decided by one architectural choice**, not by cleverness. The guide says outright: *"Adding Entire only for tracking, without using its context, checkpoints or graph evidence to improve the product, will not qualify."* Most teams build a product, then bolt on `entire graph search` and four commits. Gate inverts it — the checkpoint is the *input type* and the graph is the *evidence engine*. That's a ~30 point differential, and it's free if you make the right call at 9:35.

**The other 20 (Problem + innovation) is where "change-risk analysis" hurts you.** It's the first bullet in the Track 2 list. Half the room builds it. So the innovation points come from one of these four, ranked by what I think they're actually worth:

1. **"Did the agent do what it said?"** — the intent question. This is bullet 5 in Track 2 (*combining graph findings with checkpoint intent*) and almost nobody takes it, because it requires understanding both systems. It's also the failure mode everyone in that room has personally experienced: the agent "fixed the test" and quietly touched three other files.
2. **"Unchecked ≠ passing."** A named failure mode that no other tool draws. Intellectually the sharpest thing on the table.
3. **Falsifiability.** Every finding anchored, `--explain` shows the path, invite a judge to break it. Only safe because there's no LLM.
4. **It blocks.** A terminal that refuses your push is memorable in a register that a UI demo isn't.

The bet I'm driving: **risk is the substance, intent is the framing.** You must build blast radius — it's the spine and it's where the graph points live. But you *lead* with intent, because "another change-risk tool" and "does the agent do what it says" are the same code and completely different pitches.

**Two cheap things I want to put on the table that aren't in either doc:**

- **`gate audit`** — repo-wide, no diff needed: every symbol with dependents and zero tests, ranked. Falls out almost free once index + coverage exist (~20 min). It's a second, standalone demo artifact: *"here's your risk debt."*
- **Run Gate on a real open PR in `entireio/cli` during the demo.** Scout for a good one at lunch. If it finds something real on an upstream repo you didn't write, that's the most credible 20 seconds of your presentation. Zero build cost. Small chance it finds nothing interesting — which is why you scout first.

CONTEXT presents the one-direction architecture as a testability/demoability argument. **Green:**
- Clone is via the Entire mirror on `aws-ap-south-1` (India region) ✅

**🔴 Fix before anyone commits:**

1. **`entire status` says: "7 Codex hook(s) need approval · open /hooks"** — this is the highest-priority item on your board. If B2/B3 commit through Codex with unapproved hooks, **those commits get no checkpoint**. That's a direct hit on the 15-point Checkpoints row, and it's silent — you'd find out at 2:45. Approve them now.
2. **Worktree binding.** If B2/B3 work in separate git worktrees, their commits are **not linked to the session** — no trailer, absent from `entire checkpoint list`, and `entire doctor` reports nothing wrong. AGENTS.md documents this. Either keep all three in the primary clone on separate files, or run `entire session adopt <id> --from <primary>` in each worktree *before the first commit*. My recommendation: **one clone, separate files** — the layering makes conflicts near-zero anyway.
3. **"1 checkpoint not yet on origin"** — it syncs on `git push origin`. Push early and test one checkpoint link in a signed-out browser *today, before noon*, not at 2:55.

# 2. Recon: the API map

All four questions answered with real signatures.

### (a) Entity diff — fully exported, reusable


```go

type FileChange   struct { Path, OldPath, Status, Language string; Changes []EntityChange }  // :80

    Type string   // added | removed | renamed | signature_changed | body_changed
    Kind, Name, OldName, NewName, OldSignature, NewSignature string

    DependentsCount int      // ← ALREADY COMPUTED
```

**Two things fall out of this for free that both docs budgeted hours for:**
- `--checkpoint <id>` is ~3 lines, not a post-noon stretch goal. `AnalyzeCheckpoint` already exists.

# 3. The decisive finding — and it's a gift

I ran a full snapshot (17.6s, 69,613 records) and histogrammed every relation:

| Relation | Count |
|---|---|
| CALLS | 22,616 |
| DEFINES | 11,397 |
| DATA_FLOWS | 5,942 |
| **SIMILAR_TO** | **3,479** |
| USES_TYPE | 2,853 |
| **FILE_CHANGES_WITH** | **57** |
| **TESTS** | **9** |

**`TESTS` resolves 9 edges against 11,397 definitions in a repo with ~450 test files.** Why: the heuristic is *"test name maps to the unit under test by convention"* — `TestAnalyzeGitRange` → `AnalyzeGitRange`. Go tests here are named `TestGoReceiverMethodResolvesAcrossPackageFiles`, which names no symbol. `capabilities --json` also omits `TESTS` from Go's `relation_support_by_language` entirely.

So: **graph-native test coverage is unusable on this repo, and I have the number to prove it.**

This is not a problem. This is your best line of the day:

> *"The graph's TESTS relation resolves 9 symbols out of 11,397 in this repository. We measured it. That's exactly why Gate reports **unchecked** as a first-class state instead of pretending a symbol is covered. A gate with no test isn't passing — it's unchecked."*

That's a **measured** claim about the limits of your own evidence source, made by your own tool, on the repo you're standing in. Every other team will present the graph as an oracle. You'll present a number showing where it isn't — and a design that already handles it. That's the difference between "we used the graph" and "we understood the graph," and it's worth points in both the Graph row (15) and Problem/Innovation (20).

**Two corrections to both your docs that follow from this:**
- Both say *"use `fast` for risk."* Wrong here — `fast` emits only CALLS/CONSTRUCTS/CONTAINS/DEFINES/IMPORTS/CONFIGURES/HANDLES_ROUTE/HANDLES_TOOL/RESOURCE_DEPENDS_ON. **No** USES_TYPE, PARAM_TYPE, RETURNS_TYPE, DATA_FLOWS, FILE_CHANGES_WITH, TESTS, SIMILAR_TO. **Gate must run `full`.** 17.6s is fine, and `entire graph index` can warm it.

`SIMILAR_TO` — 3,479 edges, `reason: "near-duplicate symbol body (MinHash estimate)"`, confidence 1.0. Real example from this repo: `_safe_id` is near-identical across four client files.

⭐ Do you agree the moat is "did the agent do what it said," or do you think there's a sharper framing I'm missing?Why "did the agent do what it said" is the weaker framing
It checks a claim against a claim. The agent's self-report is the least trustworthy artifact in the room. If an agent is wrong about what it did, it's usually also wrong about what it said it would do. Building your headline on comparing those two makes your ground truth the same system you're auditing.

It requires an LLM, which kills claim #1. "I refactored auth and updated the tests" is natural language. Deterministically checking that against an entity-level diff isn't possible — you'd need a model to interpret intent. That directly contradicts "no LLM in the loop, same commit same verdict." And it invites the worst possible judge question at 2:50 PM: "so how do you compare the stated intent to the diff?" Either answer hurts you.

It's the obvious framing, which means several teams will arrive at it. It's also brittle: it does nothing when the agent said nothing, and nothing for human commits.

The sharper framing
It's already in your doc — you just haven't named it. Two sentences are doing the work:

"The graph says what structurally depends on the change; history says what habitually accompanies it."
"An empty selection is not evidence."

What those have in common: none of Gate's evidence comes from the agent. Blast radius comes from the code graph. Companion gaps come from the repo's own commit history. Coverage comes from the test tree. Not one input is the agent's description of its work.

An agent cannot make Gate say keep by describing its work well.

That's the moat, and I'd put that sentence in BUILDATHON.md. It's a one-liner, it's falsifiable on the spot, and it turns your determinism claim from a technical detail into the reason the tool can be trusted at all.

The second half is the absence framing: every other tool reports what it found. Gate reports what nobody looked at — where "nobody" means the agent, the developer, and the test suite. unchecked isn't a gap in your product; it's the product. That's why the trichotomy is your strongest idea and shouldn't be buried in §4.

Combined pitch:

Git shows what changed. Gate shows what that change put at risk and what nobody checked — using only evidence the agent didn't produce.

Two things this buys you that intent-checking doesn't: it works on human commits too (so "what happens when agents get better?" has an answer), and it's structural, not semantic — Gate supplies exactly the context an agent couldn't have had, because callers, co-change history, and coverage are invisible from inside the file being edited.

The practical point, given it's 10:30
This reframe requires zero code changes. Blast radius, companion gaps, and coverage are already agent-independent — you built the right thing and described it slightly wrong. It's a rewrite of the BUILDATHON.md opening and the pitch line, nothing more. That's why I'd take it: all upside, no build cost, on a day where build cost is everything.

What's worth keeping from the intent idea
One cheap, deterministic slice: if the Entire checkpoint records intended files or symbols in any structured form, diff that against what actually changed. That's a real "said vs did" check with no model involved. Ship it as a fourth finding type if you have slack after 2:15 — but don't put it in the pitch, and don't let it become the headline. It's a feature; the evidence-provenance argument is the moat.

You're right, and I'll take it. One correction to your reasoning first, because it changes what you can say later.

## Where your argument is slightly off — and why it doesn't matter

> "It requires an LLM... Deterministically checking that against an entity-level diff isn't possible."

Not quite. My proposal was `sem.SearchRepository(intentText)` → ranked symbols by score → join against changed entities. `SearchRepository` is a deterministic lexical+graph ranker. No model. Same bytes every run. The determinism claim would have survived literally.

**But your conclusion is right anyway, for a better reason than the one you gave.** The determinism survives; the *credibility* doesn't. When the judge asks "how do you compare stated intent to the diff?", the honest answer is "we run a keyword-and-graph similarity ranker over the sentence." That's defensible for thirty seconds and then it isn't:

- *"So if my commit message is 'fix bug', everything is unexplained?"* — yes.
- *"So if I rename the function to match my message, it passes?"* — basically, yes.

A deterministic heuristic that's weak under inspection is worse than no feature, because it's the one thing you'd have invited them to inspect. Your instinct was right; the mechanism argument just needs to be "it's a thin heuristic," not "it needs an LLM." Say the wrong version at 2:50 and someone who's read the code will correct you.

Your point 1 is the one I hadn't seen and it's the strongest: the diff is ground truth, but the agent's sentence sets *the scope of what counts as explained*. A confused agent widens its own permission. That's a real hole and it's structural, not fixable with better ranking.

And point 3 — human commits — is what actually closes it. "What happens when agents get better?" is a question you will get, and provenance answers it while intent has nothing to say.

Your line as written has one seam:

> "using only evidence the agent didn't produce"

The agent *did* produce the code. The graph is parsed from files the agent wrote. Someone will pull that thread. The precise version:

> **Gate never asks the agent what it did.**

That's airtight, and it's shorter. The distinction isn't who produced the artifacts — it's that Gate reads **artifacts, never assertions**. The 14 callers of the changed symbol were written by other people at other times; the agent can't invent them, and if it deletes them that's in the diff too. History predates the session entirely. That's the real argument, and it's stronger than the version that overclaims.

**One hole you should name before a judge finds it:** the agent could write a test that asserts nothing, and Gate would count the symbol as covered. Name it yourself — the rubric rewards disclosed limits.

Except you may not have to. I saw this in recon:

```
internal/sem/search_covertest.go:726  func searchCoveringTestBodyAsserts(lines []string, symbol SymbolRecord) bool
```

The covering-test machinery already distinguishes a test that asserts from one that doesn't. If that's reachable from `SearchResponse` — I'll verify — you get a third state for free:

```
VERIFIED    — a test covers it and asserts something
UNCHECKED   — no test covers it
UNASSERTED  — a test covers it and asserts nothing
```

That closes the one gap in the provenance claim, using the repo's own primitive, and "a test that asserts nothing is not coverage, it's decoration" is the same sentence as "an empty selection is not evidence." Same idea, one level deeper.

## What this does to the plan — better than you think

Drop intent and the four remaining signals share a property I hadn't noticed until you made the argument:

| Signal | Evidence source | Agent could fake it? |
|---|---|---|
| Blast radius | code graph (CALLS, USES_TYPE, …) — 22,616 edges | No — callers predate the change |
| Coverage / unchecked | test tree, via the repo's own build files | Only by writing a fake test → `UNASSERTED` catches it |
| Companion gap | git history — `FILE_CHANGES_WITH` + `git log` | No — history predates the session |
| Clone drift | `SIMILAR_TO`, MinHash near-duplicate bodies — 3,479 edges | No |

**Four independent evidence sources, none of them the agent's account.** That's not a pitch you're constructing after the fact — it's a property of the architecture, and it's checkable line by line. That's much better than what I proposed.

Clone drift in particular now earns its place rather than being a novelty: *"you changed one of four near-identical copies; three still have the old body and nobody looked at them."* That's literally an absence finding. It belongs in the headline set, not as a stretch.

So the story compresses to one diagram — four evidence sources, one verdict, zero inputs from the agent — which is also much easier to deliver in 90 seconds than a five-signal list.

That last line is the close, not the opening.

## What the issue actually is

**In one sentence:** Entire's checkpoints are created by hook scripts, Codex refuses to run hook scripts it hasn't been told to trust, and nothing on this machine has ever told it to.

The longer version:

1. Entire writes 7 hook scripts into the repo at [.codex/hooks.json](.codex/hooks.json) — they fire on session start, prompt submit, tool use, stop, session end. **These hooks are what create checkpoints.** No hooks firing = no checkpoints.
2. Codex has a safety rule: a repo can ship arbitrary shell in a hooks file, so Codex won't execute any of them until you approve them once per machine. Approval is stored as a `trusted_hash` in your Codex config.
3. `~/.codex/config.toml` has **no trust entries at all** — that review has never run here.
4. The dangerous part: an unapproved hook doesn't error. It just doesn't run. Everything looks fine, `entire doctor` says git hooks are OK, and the work simply never appears in `entire checkpoint list`.

That's 15 of 100 points, failing silently.

## But here's what I found digging further

**Codex is not installed on this machine.**

```
codex          not found
codex-cli      not found
openai-codex   not found
npm globals    none
```

The `~/.codex/` folder that exists is from an Electron desktop app (June, has window bounds and onboarding state) — unrelated to the Codex CLI.

So on *this* laptop the warning is currently harmless: no Codex means no Codex sessions means nothing to miss. `entire enable` registered `codex` as an agent and wrote the hooks file optimistically, and doctor is flagging the gap.

**The real exposure is on your teammates' machines**, not this one. The hooks file is committed to the repo, so anyone who clones it and runs Codex inherits those 7 unapproved hooks and starts losing checkpoints from their first commit.

## What you need to do

That depends on something I can't determine from here — and it affects the build plan, because my three-lane split put two builders on Codex.

Each teammate who will use Codex needs, on their own machine, in their own Entire clone:

```sh
# 1. install the Codex CLI (whatever your team's install path is)
# 2. clone through Entire, not git — the mirror workflow
entire repo clone /gh/anisha-singhal/entire-graph
# 3. enable with codex as the agent
entire enable -y --agent codex
# 4. open Codex in the repo, run /hooks, approve all 7:
#    session_start, session_end, user_prompt_submit, stop,
#    post_tool_use, subagent_start, subagent_stop
# 5. verify — this line must flip from REVIEW NEEDED to a checkmark
entire doctor
# 6. make one throwaway commit and confirm it registers
entire checkpoint list
```

Step 6 is the one people skip and it's the only one that actually proves it works.

If **nobody** is going to use Codex, the clean fix is one command here — `entire agent remove codex` — which deletes the hooks file and the warning with it. Don't leave a registered agent nobody uses; it's a trap for whoever clones next.

# Gate — plan

**Buildathon 2026 (Bengaluru Tech Week) · Track 2: Build with Graph Intelligence**
Fork: `anisha-singhal/entire-graph` · Entire mirror region: `aws-ap-south-1` (India)

---

## 1. One sentence

`entire graph gate` turns an agent-written pull request into a ranked reading order and a
keep / continue / revert verdict, using only evidence the agent did not produce.

---

## 2. User and problem

**User:** a developer who has to decide whether an AI agent's checkpoint is safe to merge.

A human PR is three files because a human got tired. An agent PR is forty files because the
agent did not. The reviewer has two options today:

1. Read all forty — which destroys the reason the agent was used at all.
2. Skim and approve — which is how regressions ship.

Git tells you *which lines* changed. It does not tell you what those lines can break, which of
them anyone verified, or which forty-first file everybody forgot. Nobody has a third option.

**Gate is the third option.** It reads the entity-level semantic diff, computes what structurally
depends on the change, resolves which tests actually cover it, and checks what the repository's
own history says should have changed alongside. It emits a verdict, an exit code, and — the part
a reviewer actually uses — a ranked list of which four of the forty entities deserve their eyes.

---

## 3. The moat — why this is not another change-risk tool

Every finding Gate emits comes from an artifact, never from an assertion.

| Signal | Evidence source | Can the agent fake it? |
|---|---|---|
| Blast radius | code graph — CALLS, USES_TYPE, PARAM_TYPE, RETURNS_TYPE, DATA_FLOWS | No. The callers predate the change and were written by other people. |
| Coverage / unchecked | the repository's test tree and its own build files | Only by writing a test that asserts nothing — which is why `UNASSERTED` is on the roadmap. |
| Companion gap | git history — `FILE_CHANGES_WITH` edges + `git log` | No. History predates the session entirely. |
| Clone drift | `SIMILAR_TO` — MinHash near-duplicate symbol bodies | No. |

**Gate never asks the agent what it did.**

That single sentence is the product. An agent cannot make Gate say `keep` by describing its work
well, because Gate never reads the description. This is also why the tool can block a push: a
reviewer that changes its mind is not a gate, and anything with a model in the loop changes its
mind. Run Gate twice on the same commit and diff the bytes — they are identical.

The second half of the idea is **absence**. Every other review tool reports what it found. Gate
reports what nobody looked at — where "nobody" means the agent, the developer, and the test
suite. `unchecked` is not a hole in the product. It is the product.

> **Pitch:** Your agent wrote a 47-file PR. Gate tells you which 4 to read, and what nobody checked.

### Why intent-checking was rejected

An earlier design led with "did the agent do what it said?" — comparing the checkpoint's stated
intent against the entity diff. It was dropped deliberately, and the reasoning is recorded here
because a judge will ask:

1. **It checks a claim against a claim.** The diff is ground truth, but the agent's sentence sets
   the scope of what counts as *explained*. A confused agent widens its own permission.
2. **The mechanism is thin under inspection.** It would have been deterministic — `SearchRepository`
   is a lexical + graph ranker with no model — but "we run keyword similarity over the commit
   message" does not survive the follow-up question *"so if I write 'fix bug', everything is
   unexplained?"* Yes, it would be.
3. **It does nothing for human commits**, and nothing when the agent said nothing.
4. **Verified: there is no structured intent to read.** `sem.Result` carries only the checkpoint ID.
   `entire checkpoint explain` returns prose. A deterministic structured said-vs-did check has no
   input to work from in this system.

Provenance answers what intent could not: *"what happens when agents get better?"* Gate still
works, because it never depended on the agent in the first place.

---

## 4. Why Entire is essential

**The checkpoint is the input. The graph is the evidence engine. Remove either and there is no
product.**

- `entire graph gate --checkpoint <id>` resolves a checkpoint to a commit range through
  `gitutil.FindCommitWithCheckpoint` and `sem.AnalyzeCheckpoint`. The checkpoint is a first-class
  input type, not a way of naming a SHA.
- Three of the four signals are graph traversals over relation records. Delete the graph and Gate
  has nothing to report.

This is not Entire bolted onto a product for the sake of the rules. It is the substrate.

---

## 5. Architecture

One direction, no loops. Every layer passes forward and never calls back.

```
  --checkpoint <id> | --base <ref> --head <ref>
                │
                ▼
        ┌───────────────┐
        │    collect    │   the ONLY impure layer
        └───────┬───────┘   sem.AnalyzeCheckpoint / AnalyzeGitRange
                │           sem.BuildProviderSnapshotWithOptions
                ▼           sem.SearchRepository
        ┌───────────────┐
        │     index     │   reverse-edge map, file→symbol map,
        └───────┬───────┘   keyed by compound-v1 symbol IDs
                │
    ┌───────────┼───────────┬───────────┐
    ▼           ▼           ▼           ▼
  risk      coverage   companions    clones      pure functions, no I/O
    │           │           │           │
    └───────────┴─────┬─────┴───────────┘
                      ▼
              ┌───────────────┐
              │    verdict    │   pure: findings → verdict + exit code
              └───────┬───────┘
                      ▼
              ┌───────────────┐
              │    render     │   text | --json | review order
              └───────────────┘
```

Two reasons this shape, both load-bearing:

1. **It is a parallelization plan.** Layers that never call back are three people editing disjoint
   files behind one struct contract. This is the only way four signals fit in the time available.
2. **The noon curveball lands in one place.** A constraint about output, thresholds, or verdict
   semantics touches `verdict` or `render` — both pure, both unit-tested with synthetic records,
   neither requiring CGO to test.

### Package layout

| Path | Contents | CGO needed to test? |
|---|---|---|
| `internal/gate/` | `types.go`, `index.go`, `risk.go`, `coverage.go`, `companions.go`, `clones.go`, `verdict.go`, `render.go` | **No** |
| `internal/cli/gate.go` | flag parsing, `resolveRepo`, all `sem.*` calls | Yes |
| `internal/cli/root.go` | one `case "gate":` in the dispatch switch | — |
| `internal/cli/help.go` | one `commandDocs` entry (auto-wires `gate --help`) | — |

The `internal/gate` boundary means a builder whose laptop cannot compile tree-sitter can still
write and test two thirds of the product.

---

## 6. How we use the Entire Graph — in detail

This section is the answer to "show where the evidence came from."

### 6.1 Which APIs we call, and why in-process

All calls are **in-process Go**, not shell-outs to `entire graph`. The track rules say an
integration that merely calls an Entire command from another interface is not sufficient; Gate is
a subcommand *of the provider*, reusing its internals.

```go
// entity-level semantic diff — internal/sem/analyze.go
func AnalyzeCheckpoint(ctx, repo, checkpointID string) (Result, error)          // :1159
func AnalyzeGitRange(ctx, repo, base, head string, paths []string) (Result, error)

// checkpoint → commit — internal/gitutil/git.go
func FindCommitWithCheckpoint(ctx, repo, checkpointID string) (string, error)   // :146

// symbols + relations — internal/sem/provider.go
func BuildProviderSnapshotWithOptions(ctx, repo, ver string, o ProviderSnapshotOptions) (ProviderSnapshot, error)  // :929

// ranked search, covering tests, runnable verify command — internal/sem/search.go
func SearchRepository(ctx, repo, providerVersion, query string, o SearchOptions) (SearchResponse, error)  // :683
```

`EntityChange.DependentsCount` arrives already populated by `internal/sem/dependents.go`, so the
first cut of the risk signal costs nothing.

### 6.2 Which relations each signal traverses

Measured on this repository at `HEAD = 3a2a715`, full profile, 69,613 records, **17.6 s**:

| Relation | Count | Used by |
|---|---:|---|
| `CALLS` | 22,616 | risk |
| `DEFINES` | 11,397 | index |
| `DATA_FLOWS` | 5,942 | risk (depth 2) |
| `SIMILAR_TO` | 3,479 | **clone drift** |
| `USES_TYPE` | 2,853 | risk (type consumers) |
| `IMPORTS` | 2,286 | index, coverage fallback |
| `READS_FIELD` | 1,592 | risk |
| `PARAM_TYPE` | 1,504 | risk |
| `RETURNS_TYPE` | 993 | risk |
| `CONSTRUCTS` | 71 | risk |
| `FILE_CHANGES_WITH` | 57 | **companion gap** |
| `TESTS` | **9** | *unusable — see 6.4* |

### 6.3 Gate must run `--profile full`

`fast` emits only `CALLS, CONFIGURES, CONSTRUCTS, CONTAINS, DEFINES, HANDLES_ROUTE, HANDLES_TOOL,
IMPORTS, RESOURCE_DEPENDS_ON`. It has **no** `USES_TYPE`, `PARAM_TYPE`, `RETURNS_TYPE`,
`DATA_FLOWS`, `FILE_CHANGES_WITH`, `TESTS`, or `SIMILAR_TO` — which is three of our four signals.
17.6 s is acceptable; `entire graph index --head --profile full` warms a durable cache for
repeated runs.

### 6.4 The measured finding that shapes the whole design

**`TESTS` resolves 9 edges against 11,397 definitions in this repository.**

The heuristic is *"test name maps to the unit under test by convention"* — `TestAnalyzeGitRange`
→ `AnalyzeGitRange`. Real Go test names here look like
`TestGoReceiverMethodResolvesAcrossPackageFiles`, which names no symbol. `capabilities --json`
also omits `TESTS` from Go's `relation_support_by_language` entirely.

So graph-native test coverage is unusable on this repo, and **we have the number**.

This is not a problem to hide. It is the reason `unchecked` exists as a first-class verdict state
rather than a footnote:

> The graph's TESTS relation resolves 9 symbols out of 11,397 in this repository. We measured it.
> That is exactly why Gate reports **unchecked** instead of pretending a symbol is covered.
> A gate with no test is not passing — it is unchecked.

Graph results are evidence, not an oracle. Gate is built around a measured statement of where its
own evidence runs out.

**Consequence:** the coverage signal does not use `TESTS` edges. It uses the covering-test
machinery already inside `search` (`internal/sem/search_covertest.go`), reached through
`SearchRepository`, which resolves tests by mirror-path, name convention, and body mention — and
which demonstrably works on this repo. `SearchResponse` hands back both:

- `CoverageNote *SearchCoverageNote` — `{Symbol, Total, Peers, More, FilePath}`
- `VerifyCommand *SearchVerifyCommand` — `{Command, Targets, DerivedFrom, Tier, RunnerMissing}`,
  a runnable command derived from the repo's own build files, with its own confidence tier
  (`narrow` / `suite` / `build-check` / `none`)

We do not write a test resolver. We consume one that already covers go, pytest, npm, cargo, maven,
gradle, composer and ruby, and that reports its own uncertainty.

### 6.5 Provenance — `--explain`

`RelationRecord.Evidence[]` carries `{Kind, FilePath, StartLine, EndLine, Detail}`. Every finding
Gate prints can be expanded to the exact call path and source location behind it:

```
$ entire graph gate --explain 2
2. VerifyToken @ internal/auth/token.go:88
   ← CALLS   middleware.Require   internal/http/mw.go:41   (evidence: call_site, mw.go:44)
   ← CALLS   router.Protected     internal/http/router.go:98
   14 dependents at depth ≤2 · UNCHECKED
```

A judge can open any one of those files and check it. That invitation is only safe because there
is no model in the loop.

### 6.6 Graph evidence we record for the submission

Saved under `docs/graph-findings/`:

1. **Search / definition lookup** — the orientation queries that located the diff engine, the
   dispatch switch and the snapshot builder.
2. **Relationship / impact analysis before a high-risk change** — `entire graph impact` on the
   area touched by the noon curveball, run *before* editing.
3. **Final semantic diff** — `entire graph diff --base <pre-noon> --head HEAD --json`.
4. **Gate on itself** — Gate's verdict on our own commits, including the curveball commit.

---

## 7. The four signals

### 7.1 Risk — blast radius

For every `removed`, `renamed` or `signature_changed` entity, walk **reverse** edges over
`CALLS, ASYNC_CALLS, CONSTRUCTS, USES_TYPE, PARAM_TYPE, RETURNS_TYPE, READS_FIELD, WRITES_FIELD,
DATA_FLOWS`, depth ≤ 2, and rank by dependent count.

Depth is capped at 2 deliberately: without it, one utility function pulls in the whole repo and
the output becomes noise. `--hops 1|2` exposes the trade-off.

### 7.2 Coverage — verified / unchecked

Per changed entity, `SearchRepository` → `CoverageNote` + `VerifyCommand`. Emit one runnable test
command listing only the selected tests. Report three counts, not one:

- **verified** — a test covers it
- **unchecked** — no test covers it
- **no resolver** — the language has no derivable runner (honest, not a failure)

### 7.3 Companion gap

Files that historically co-change with the edited files but were not edited this time.
`FILE_CHANGES_WITH` edges carry the ratio already — `reason: "files changed together in 52 recent
commits"`, `evidence: [{kind: "git_log", detail: "52 commits"}]` — so the "14/15 past commits"
phrasing comes straight from the data. Only 57 such edges exist here, so `git log --name-only -n 200`
widens the set with a ≥ 70% / min-5-observation threshold.

*The graph says what structurally depends on the change; history says what habitually accompanies
it. Bugs hide in the gap between those two views.*

`SIMILAR_TO` (3,479 edges, `reason: "near-duplicate symbol body (MinHash estimate)"`,
confidence 1.0). If a changed symbol has near-duplicate siblings that did **not** change, say so:

> `_safe_id` changed. 3 near-duplicate siblings did not: `cmm_client.py:29`,
> `entire_client.py:31`, `graphify_client.py:28`.

*You fixed the bug in one copy. Three copies still have it.* This is an absence finding — exactly
the shape of the product — and it uses a relation type nobody else will touch.

## 8. Verdict model

Four states. Mirror-style honesty about the failure case, without Mirror's seven codes.

| Exit | Verdict | Meaning |
|---:|---|---|
| 0 | `keep` | Verified. Ship it. |
| 1 | `continue` | Mostly fine — check these specific things. |
| 2 | `revert` | Something is wrong. Roll back. |
| 5 | `unusable` | Gate ran, here is the full report, nothing downstream can build on it. |

`unusable` exists because when the graph cannot parse a file or the language has no test resolver,
the honest answer is *"we could not check"* — not `revert`, which is a false accusation.

**The rule is printed in every run**, so the tool is never a black box:

```
RULE  revert  = a removed or signature-changed entity with ≥1 dependent AND no covering test
      continue = risky change with tests, OR a companion gap, OR new entities with no tests
      keep     = none of the above
      unusable = the graph could not produce evidence for the changed files
```

Colour carries verdict only. Everything else is plain.

The verdict decides *whether*. The review order decides *what to read*. Same computation, sorted


your eyes.

gracefully rather than dump.
